sources.name: FDEP Public Notices of Pollution (s. 403.077, F.S.)
sources.what: Every reportable pollution release filed since July 2017: incident number, release start and end, facility, county, coordinates, free-text report

sources.name: EAGLE-I county outage record
sources.holder: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
sources.what: Customers without power per county every 15 minutes, 2014 to 2025, with the customer count per county (MCC)
sources.records: about 1.0 to 1.2 million Florida records a year; 11.19 million customers

sources.name: FCC DIRS communications status reports
sources.holder: Federal Communications Commission, Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau
sources.what: Daily PDF per activated hurricane: cell sites served and out of service by county; from 2020 the cause split (damage, transport, power) and sites on backup power

sources.name: NOAA nClimGrid-Daily county averages
sources.holder: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
sources.what: Daily county-average precipitation (mm) and mean temperature; the file id is the NCEI state code (08 for Florida) plus county number, not the FIPS
sources.records: 67 counties, every day July 2017 to August 2026

sources.name: HURDAT2 Atlantic best track
sources.what: Six-hourly positions and intensities; landfall points

sources.name: OpenFEMA
sources.what: Disaster declarations (counties with Individual Assistance), Hazard Mitigation Assistance projects (type, approval, closure, federal share), Public Assistance funded projects (category, applicant, county, obligation), IHP registrations
sources.records: 828 mitigation projects and 344 category B wastewater projects for the nine storms

sources.name: Companion restoration study (track exposure, surge, damage rate, t80)
sources.what: County maximum wind, peak surge, FEMA registration rate and hours to restore 80 percent for seven storms

sources.name: Rules and programs cited
sources.what: Power outage contingency plan rule (62-600.705, F.A.C.), Clean Waterways Act 2020, emergency procurement (s. 287.057), FlaWARN mutual aid, AHCA generator rule

stages.purpose: a01_pnp_incidents: clean and classify the FDEP Public Notices of Pollution (section 403.077, F.S.) into an incident table and a county-day series (blueprint P5 section 4).
a02_outage_exposure: EAGLE-I county outages reduced to county-day exposure measures for every day 2017-07-01 to 2025-12-31 (the Public Notice era), the denominator of the cascade.
a03_cascade_panel: the county-day panel of the power-to-water cascade for the nine Public-Notice-era hurricanes (blueprint P5 sections 2 and 4; RQ1 and the first look at RQ2 and RQ4).
a04_dose_response: count models of the power-to-water cascade (blueprint P5 RQ2 dose-response, RQ3 learning, RQ4 silent-county correction).
a05_cause_and_volume: what the notices say caused the release, where it went, and how much (blueprint P5 RQ5), by storm window and for the baseline.

a06_swfl_replication: reproduce the Lee and Collier numbers of Nguyen and Tsegaye (2022, Construction Research Congress, "Vulnerability of Southwest Florida Water Infrastructure under the Impacts of Hurricane") from the 2026 pull of the same FDEP dataset, as the validation table of the paper (blueprint P5 section 4, stage a06; Gate 1 in its published form).

a07_florida_map: the geographic layers for the study-area figure (manuscript Fig 1): per storm, the county window's outage exposure and excess sewer releases, plus the HURDAT2 tracks of the nine Public-Notice-era hurricanes and the landfall points.
a08_reporting_gap: how long after a release the notice was filed, by storm and by county-window, and whether the filing lag grows with the outage (blueprint P5 RQ4, Gate 3).

a09_cascade_clock: the clocks of the cascade. Release start times in the notices are date-only (every stamp is midnight), so the hour of the release is unknown; the FILING time is real, and the release and end DATES are real. Four clocks follow.

a10_silence_index: how dark the record goes, where, and by how much (the RQ4 headline made general). Observed against model-expected releases for every county-window, the probability that a record goes dark as a function of the outage, the cascade ledger per storm, and the same test on the outage record itself.

a11_wind_or_wire: is it the wind or the wire? The hurricane reaches the sewer through several channels: wind and surge damage the stations directly, rain and surge flood the collection system, and the outage stops the pumps. This stage asks how much of the release count the outage carries once the storm's physical exposure is in the model, whether the SPEED of restoration matters beyond the customer- hours, whether the ownership of the grid matters, and which counties cascade most per customer (the propensity map).

a12_repeat_strike: the same county, struck twice. Model B (a04) compares slopes across storms with county fixed effects; this stage makes the comparison county by county for the pairs of storms that hit the same counties, from thirteen days apart (Helene then Milton, 2024) to seven years (Irma 2017 then Milton 2024). If generators and hardening reached the lift stations between the strikes, the second strike should produce fewer releases per customer-hour of outage in the same county.

a13_release_geography: where the releases are. Every notice carries coordinates; this stage cleans them, places each storm-window sewer release on the map, measures its distance to the storm's track, and builds the release profile with distance from the track for each storm, against the outage profile on the same axis.

a14_volume_regimes: how much, and who carries it. The count of releases is the paper's outcome because it is complete; the volume is stated in about six notices in ten and is dominated by a few plant discharges. This stage measures that concentration and asks whether the volume, where stated, follows the outage dose the way the count does.

a15_recovery_autonomy: who ends the spill, the operator or the grid? The county's share of customers without power on the day a release ended (a09) cannot tell a station whose own feeder came back from a station a crew rescued with a generator while the county stayed dark. The notice narrative can: operators write "generator installed", "bypass pumping", "pumper trucks" or "power was restored". This stage reads the END cause from the narrative and measures recovery autonomy, the resilience construct of the paper's reframing (blueprint v2 of 2026-09-06).

a16_cellular_dependency: the second dependent lifeline. The same grid failure, read against cell sites out of service by county from the FCC's DIRS reports, on the four constructs of the reframed paper: propagation (how much of the outage reaches the cell sites), buffering (batteries: does the cell outage lag the power outage by a day), recovery autonomy (does the cell network come back before the grid), and adaptation (has the slope changed from Irma to Milton). The FCC states the cause of each outage (damage, transport, power), which the wastewater notices only give in free text.

a17_resilience_signature: the two dependent lifelines on the four constructs of the reframed paper, side by side, from results already computed upstream. Nothing new is estimated here; this stage assembles the comparison table that is the paper's central exhibit.

a18_adaptation_lag: why the dependency has not moved. The paper's adaptation construct found no fall in the outage-to-release slope from 2017 to 2024 (a04, a12). This stage asks whether the money that buys decoupling, FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) awards for generators and for water and sewer protective measures, had arrived by the time the next hurricane struck, and measures the emergency response that Public Assistance (PA) reimbursed in each county-window (the machinery behind recovery autonomy, a15).
